name: Language learning
summary: Why finished lessons don’t always help you start speaking — and how to link the conversation, the explanation of the mistake and the next attempt.
lead:
One person knows the words but freezes when an answer is needed without a prompt. Another has already spoken the language and, after a break, is made to go through the greetings again. The number of exercises completed says little about how well the studying serves their particular goal.

We look at three answers: start from a specific gap, make room for the person’s own speech, and bring the corrections back in new conversations. Along the way we look at when a standalone tool is useful and when it merely adds one more piece to learning that is already scattered.

audiencesArt.alt: Different jobs in the “Language learning” category.

audiences.title: Speak more freely in a familiar situation
audiences.body: A person can pick a ready-made answer but is slow to build their own. They need a situation where they can ask for clarification, rephrase a thought and finish speaking without being held to a single stock line.

audiences.title: Come back to a language already learned
audiences.body: Individual words and forms have to be recalled while quick access to familiar material is kept. Repeating the whole course costs time, and a single overall test may miss the difference between reading and speaking.

audiences.title: Understand the family and a particular language environment
audiences.body: For talking with relatives, familiar topics and the variety of the language matter; for understanding a favorite series, it is the spoken sound. These jobs help choose the material, but they don’t replace a check of what the person can already do.

sections.title: Start from your own job
sections.intro: A new language, a return after a break and a single gap each call for a different entry point.

observations.title: Close one gap
passages: A person can be learning vocabulary confidently and still get lost in the writing system. A review about Japanese values exactly that separate work on kanji. A tool like this belongs next to a course if it drills what a general lesson never reaches.

Another example is Spanish verb forms that felt frightening to approach. Here a level marks a topic learned and helps you come back to the exercise. A rising level by itself says nothing about whether the form will work in conversation; the next task has to show that.

Separate drills can be tied together through your own material. If a word turns up in a text, it is worth saving the whole phrase and choosing what to review: recognizing the character, writing it or saying it. Importing cards is useful for exactly that link to a question that has already come up.

quotes.text: I have tried many language apps for different aspects of Japanese language, and this is the one I recommend most highly for drilling the otherwise overwhelming list of kanji into your brain, and making it stick. Worth every penny to unlock all the content.

Today, I finally felt like I could Level Up to Level 7. Before I started this app, I was afraid I'd fail with Spanish no matter how hard I tried. I was so intimidated by Spanish verbs in all the other apps (and in books), that I didn't think I'd ever get it.

This is the best flashcard app for language-learning. With attention to a few details, it would annihilate competitors. PROS: Automatically creates cards from imported or pasted text. Some apps emphasize the value of making the cards yours — this nails it.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Close one gap”.

observations.title: Learn the language for your own conversations
passages: The language you need is often tied to particular people: relatives, a host family or the people around you on a trip. So the existence of a course is only the start of the choice. What matters is the speech it lets you hear and the situations it has you live through in an exercise.

Before a long course, it is worth opening material close to your own goal: a family conversation, a familiar topic or a text you want to read. That helps judge the variety of the language, the writing and the level of the explanations. Personal interest becomes a support for choosing the content, not a reason to credit every course with the same fitness.

A conversation at the family table is not the same as ordering coffee: the topics, the pace and the habitual expressions all change. A course like that benefits from situations out of the audience’s life and from different voices. For sign language there is a further job: understanding the different ways familiar signs are performed. Individual courses may use different formats while keeping the same overall goal — talking with particular people.

quotes.text: I found this app when I was searching for some way to learn Albanian because that is where my family is from. This app had it and usually I can't find this language on any app. I was so excited thinking I can finally become actually apart of my culture.

I first started using Memrise about seven years ago to learn German before visiting cousins in Germany for the first time. This app brought me up to conversational level within only a few months, and I was able to exist almost entirely in German.

I have used JapanesePod to help me prepare for my study abroad in Japan and this app helped me connect with my host family tremendously. The GreekPod helped me before a trip to Athens earlier this year as well.

placements.title: Learn the language for your own conversations

observations.title: Come back without repeating the whole course
passages: Coming back to a language is not the same as meeting it for the first time. A person may recognize words and read while building an answer slowly; may remember the writing system but not particular forms. Being made to go through every beginner lesson spends time on things they can already do.

A map of separate skills helps, with the option to try the exercises and move on to the gaps. Skipping the familiar shouldn’t mean closing off access to it for good. Coming back has to stay under control: today go over a difficult spot, then move on, keeping the option of checking against the basics.

Instead of a single level label, it helps to show separate results: reading comes easily, listening is harder, answering runs short of verb forms. A person can start with one difficulty and go back to the basics as needed. The test of a product like this is exercises before and after the practice, not just lessons completed.

quotes.text: I used to speak French conversationally and went many years without practicing. I've been trying to practice again, but I've found frustration with other language learning apps because they force me through lessons of things I already know before letting me get to where I need to be.

This is the best system for hiragana and katakana I've used. I've been needing to freshen up my kana and it not only quickly put me back into shape, but introduced many words I didn't previously know in the language!

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Come back without repeating the whole course”.

placements.title: Come back without repeating the whole course

sections.title: Say it yourself and understand the answer
sections.intro: Practice begins where a person puts together a line of their own. After that, what matters is the time to answer and a clear breakdown of what was heard.

observations.title: Make room for the person’s own line
passages: A conversation with a teacher gives a human response and work on a personal goal. A rehearsal with an app can be convenient where embarrassment gets in the way or a partner is hard to find. The two formats are valuable in different circumstances, and a person may use both.

The main question to ask of a speaking exercise is whether you can say something of your own and get a connected answer. If the practice comes down to guessing the prepared line, it helps rehearse the scene but leaves little room for speech of your own. It helps to choose topics where familiar words have to be assembled into a new line.

A good scene allows several ways to reach the goal: check an address, ask for something to be repeated, turn an offer down. That is closer to using the language than hunting for the single prepared phrase. For a first speaking trainer, one carefully built situation can give more useful feedback than hundreds of shallow topics.

quotes.text: italki is, without a doubt, one of the best language-learning platforms available today. What truly sets it apart is the human connection: real teachers, real conversations, and lessons tailored exactly to your goals and learning style.

I had human tutor before and every class made me feel like stupid person, even though tutor was kind. I have shame to speak in front of real human, my face goes red and my brain just stops. All words disappear. I stopped lessons after maybe 3 months. With this app I speak every day now without fear.

I am a B2 French speaker and bought this because I am shy and hate speaking in public, and my wife, who is much more fluent that I am will rarely speak to me in French for more than a few minutes and she is a terrible teacher. I tried a bunch of apps and this is the only one that let me actually practice speaking.

placements.title: Make room for the person’s own line

observations.title: Show what was heard first
passages: Before grading pronunciation, the app has to show what it heard. If recognition got it wrong even in a quiet room, a correction attached to a wrong transcript only confuses. A person needs access to the recording and the chance to repeat the phrase without a failed attempt being graded as language.

There is another failure: the system starts answering before the person has finished the thought. In that case correcting vocabulary or grammar is premature. First let them finish, then respond to what was said, including a request to repeat or an expression of annoyance.

When a line really has been heard, the transcript becomes material to go over. You can find the difficult spot, listen to it and try saying it differently. It is worth keeping a few such examples for the next conversation, so that the feedback doesn’t disappear when the conversation is closed.

quotes.text: This app started with promise, but quickly devolved into a frustrating experience that feels like a complete rip-off. The core functionality, voice detection, is shockingly unreliable. Even in a perfectly quiet, closed room, with absolutely no background noise, the app struggles to accurately detect my voice.

I find the follow lessons to be OK, but but it often cuts you off before you can finish your answer. The live conversation is horrible. It seems to be programmed to respond only in preset responses. I tried to tell it I was frustrated and it just kept going.

When speaking with the AI conversationally, it gives appropriate responses and is good for speaking and listening. However, it has a transcription feature where you can go back and read what you said and what the AI said. My listening is passable but my speaking needs work and this gives me a way to see where I'm failing.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Show what was heard first”.

observations.title: Hear the model and go back to the detail
passages: On the move, an audio lesson can fill the time when looking at a screen is awkward. In one review a person links their studying to the commute. What matters for this scenario is a sequence of short phrases, pauses for your own answer and an easy way back to the last line.

Repeating after the speaker does a job of its own: hearing the sound and reproducing it. One author values exactly this method while noting the limits of the course. Going back to the recording and the text helps work through a difficult spot; endless repetition without understanding leaves the question open.

But first the model itself has to be worth trusting. One author stopped trusting the AI’s corrections after hearing mistakes in its German. For a speaking product, the quality of the audio and the checking of the feedback matter more than the number of voices. The variety of the language should be stated, and a questionable correction should be open to a second check.

quotes.text: IVE been using this app now for about 4-5 months and lemme tell u sumnthing. I speak English and Montenegrin (Serbo-Croatian) natively and learned Greek and Persian through this app. I just wish they had Latin cause I learned a real good of Greek in my car on my commute.

Japanese learner here. the app is really good for shadowing. repeating phrases over and over and learning this way. with some tweaking, this could be an amazing app. I think the Pimsleur people are a little stuck in their own ideology.

I mostly do the custom scenarios and try to speak in German. The AI tutor pronounces German words incorrectly and with a clear American accent. Once I noticed that, I stopped trusting its feedback on my own pronunciation.

placements.title: Hear the model and go back to the detail

sections.title: Work it out and try again
sections.intro: An explanation becomes useful when it helps change a specific phrase and build the next one yourself.

observations.title: Explain exactly the part that wasn’t clear
passages: A person repeats a phrase without understanding the role of the individual words. The first step is to take that phrase apart: who is acting, which tense is used and what changes when the words are reordered. One positive review values having the meaning explained along with the saying of it.

The explanation has to be available at the moment of difficulty. When you have to leave the lesson to go looking for the rule, the link with your own attempt is lost. One author praises a course for explaining how the language works; that is an argument for a short explanation next to the example rather than one more screen of drills.

After the breakdown it is worth changing the tense or the participant in the original phrase and making a new one. That shows whether the rule helped. An account of a course finished without an understanding of grammar shows the risk of measuring learning only by the number of exercises completed.

quotes.text: This app is way better than Duolingo because instead of just teaching you how to say things like Duo does TEUIDA teaches you how to say it and explains what every word means!

I've only been using Babbel for a few days, but I can already tell a big difference compared to other language apps I've tried. I'm currently learning Spanish, and I feel like Babbel does a much better job of actually explaining the language rather than just having you repeat things.

This an AI driven Duolingo alternative. Albeit it is actually better than the original when it comes to learning. I've finished the entire Russian course on Duolingo and I still didn't understand almost everything. Duolingo never stops to explain any grammar rules.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Explain exactly the part that wasn’t clear”.

placements.title: Explain exactly the part that wasn’t clear

observations.title: Put the word back into a living context
passages: A dictionary can be a reading tool, not just a fast translator. A word’s history, a shade of usage and links to related concepts help explain why similar options work differently. Writing like this keeps the interest in the language itself alive.

For practical use, the link to the original question has to be kept. A word you have looked up is best read together with an example and usage labels, and then taken back to the phrase where it turned up. An authorial voice and substantive cross-references make an entry good to explore, as long as they don’t hide the main meaning.

A word from a work email is worth saving together with the sentence it came from and your own attempt at using it. At review time those links help recall why it was needed. Etymology and extra examples can deepen the interest, but the nearest meaning has to stay available without reading the whole entry.

quotes.text: I hate to sound cheesy and typical and say this is the best app ever but it is lol. I honestly use this app first and when I don't have access to the app, I use the web browser. To truly understand the definition of a word the etymology is the key.

The modern world has no shortage of dry wit, but Etymonline is both funny and incisive, making the expository paragraphs more compelling by their unique voice. The app itself is bare-bones, but easy to use. The cross-references in the entries make it easy to fall down the rabbit hole.

For so many reasons, I find it to be the best dictionary app, but especially for the note following the 2nd definition of 'literally' (adv. inf.)! I hope they won't mind it if I quote — this is the kind of nuance no other dictionary gives you.

placements.title: Put the word back into a living context

conclusion.title: First, a useful breakdown of your own speech
conclusion.body:
The most convincing priority here is to connect a line of your own with feedback you can understand and with the next attempt. The reviews contain both the wish to speak and specific obstacles: the app cuts the answer off, mishears the words or doesn’t explain the correction. Adding new topics removes none of these obstacles. The thing to do first is to carry one speaking situation through to the point where the person understands what to fix and tries it in another phrase.

Narrow trainers for the writing system, vocabulary and grammar can help alongside a route like that. But one more disconnected course is justified only where the existing learning leaves a definite gap. For a family language and for sign language, carefully chosen material matters especially; a generic level mechanic is no substitute.
